claim: The lateral prefrontal cortex is involved in the integration of multiple types of information, including working memory and motor preparation.
source: The lateral prefrontal cortex is involved in the integration of multiple types of information, including working memory and motor preparation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a background claim about LPFC function.

claim: The lateral prefrontal cortex of non-human primates contains two minimally dependent low-dimensional subspaces: one that encodes working memory information, and another that encodes motor preparation information.
source: Here, we show that the lateral prefrontal cortex of non-human primates contains two minimally dependent low-dimensional subspaces: one that encodes working memory information, and another that encodes motor preparation information.
evidence: This is the primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by the experimental data and analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: These subspaces capture all the information about the target in the delay periods.
source: These subspaces capture all the information about the target in the delay periods, and the information in both subspaces is reduced in error trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by the decoding analyses showing that target information is present in the subspaces during delay periods.

claim: The information in both subspaces is reduced in error trials.
source: These subspaces capture all the information about the target in the delay periods, and the information in both subspaces is reduced in error trials.
evidence: This is supported by the error trial analysis showing decreased decoding performance in both subspaces during error trials.

claim: A single population of neurons with mixed selectivity forms both subspaces.
source: A single population of neurons with mixed selectivity forms both subspaces, but the information is kept largely independent from each other.
evidence: This is supported by the loading weight analysis showing that the same neurons contribute to both subspaces.

claim: The information in the two subspaces is kept largely independent from each other.
source: A single population of neurons with mixed selectivity forms both subspaces, but the information is kept largely independent from each other.
evidence: This is supported by the minimal mutual information between the unmixed elements and the interference analyses.

claim: A bump attractor model with divisive normalization replicates the properties of the neural data.
source: A bump attractor model with divisive normalization replicates the properties of the neural data.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results showing that only models with divisive normalization replicate all key features of the neural data.

claim: A large proportion of neurons in the lateral prefrontal cortex encode a mixture of two or more types of information.
source: A large proportion of neurons in the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) encode a mixture of two or more of these types of information (Rigotti et al., 2013; Parthasarathy et al., 2017; Masse et al., 2019; van Ede et al., 2019; Marcos et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mixed selectivity endows the LPFC with a high-dimensional representational space.
source: This mixed selectivity endows the LPFC with a high-dimensional representational space (Rigotti et al., 2013), but it also presents the challenge of understanding how downstream regions that receive mixed-selective input from the LPFC can read out meaningful information.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rigotti et al., 2013.

claim: Multiple low-dimensional information subspaces embedded within the high-dimensional state space of LPFC could enable the independent readout of different types of information with minimal interference.
source: One possible solution would be to have multiple low-dimensional information subspaces, embedded within the high-dimensional state space of LPFC, which could enable the independent readout of different types of information with minimal interference from changes of information in other subspaces (Remington et al., 2018; Parthasarathy, 2019; Semedo et al., 2019; Mante et al., 2013; Wolff et al., 2019; Druckmann and Chklovskii, 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Information subspaces have been identified in the medial frontal cortex.
source: Information subspaces have been identified in the medial frontal cortex (Wang et al., 2018), lateral prefrontal cortex (Parthasarathy, 2019), early visual areas (Semedo et al., 2019), and motor cortex (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Information subspaces have been identified in the lateral prefrontal cortex.
source: Information subspaces have been identified in the medial frontal cortex (Wang et al., 2018), lateral prefrontal cortex (Parthasarathy, 2019), early visual areas (Semedo et al., 2019), and motor cortex (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Parthasarathy, 2019.

claim: Information subspaces have been identified in early visual areas.
source: Information subspaces have been identified in the medial frontal cortex (Wang et al., 2018), lateral prefrontal cortex (Parthasarathy, 2019), early visual areas (Semedo et al., 2019), and motor cortex (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Semedo et al., 2019.

claim: Information subspaces have been identified in motor cortex.
source: Information subspaces have been identified in the medial frontal cortex (Wang et al., 2018), lateral prefrontal cortex (Parthasarathy, 2019), early visual areas (Semedo et al., 2019), and motor cortex (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kaufman et al., 2014 and Elsayed et al., 2016.

claim: No studies to date have explicitly tested whether information about two separate cognitive processes can be simultaneously encoded in subspaces within a single biological neural network.
source: However, no studies to date have explicitly tested whether information about two separate cognitive processes can be simultaneously encoded in subspaces within a single biological neural network.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the literature, establishing the novelty of the current work.

claim: Target information emerged in the working memory subspace in Delay 1 and was maintained till the end of Delay 2.
source: Here, we demonstrate the existence of two minimally dependent information subspaces in the LPFC network: (1) a working memory subspace in which target information emerged in Delay 1, and was maintained till the end of Delay 2
evidence: This is supported by the cross-temporal decoding results in the working memory subspace.

claim: Information in the motor preparation subspace emerged only in Delay 2 after the presentation of the distractor.
source: and (2) a motor preparation subspace in which information emerged only in Delay 2 after the presentation of the distractor, possibly due to the initiation of saccade preparation after the last sensory cue that reliably predicted the timing of the Go cue (i.e. the offset of the distractor).
evidence: This is supported by the cross-temporal decoding results in the motor preparation subspace.

claim: The emergence of motor preparation information was possibly due to the initiation of saccade preparation after the last sensory cue that reliably predicted the timing of the Go cue.
source: and (2) a motor preparation subspace in which information emerged only in Delay 2 after the presentation of the distractor, possibly due to the initiation of saccade preparation after the last sensory cue that reliably predicted the timing of the Go cue (i.e. the offset of the distractor).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the timing of motor preparation activity emergence.

claim: Both subspaces exhibited behavioral relevance with significantly decreased information in error trials only in the subspace, and not in the null space.
source: Both subspaces exhibited behavioral relevance with significantly decreased information in error trials only in the subspace, and not in the null space.
evidence: This is supported by the error trial analysis showing decreased decoding performance in the subspaces but not due to general noise increase.

claim: There was a reduction in information in the memory subspace when information in the movement preparation subspace emerged.
source: Interestingly, we found a reduction in information in the memory subspace when information in the movement preparation subspace emerged.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of decoding performance in Delay 1 vs Delay 2 in the working memory subspace.

claim: The average firing rate of the neurons across the population remained unchanged between delay periods.
source: At the same time, we found that the average firing rate of the neurons across the population remained unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by the population mean firing rate analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: A normalization mechanism could have been acting on the population activity.
source: This suggested that a normalization mechanism could have been acting on the population activity (Ruff and Cohen, 2017; Duong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of constant firing rate despite changing information content, supported by citations.

claim: A bump attractor model with divisive normalization allowed replication of the observed neurophysiological properties.
source: We subsequently found that a bump attractor model (Compte et al., 2000) with divisive normalization allowed us to replicate the observed neurophysiological properties.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: 226 single neurons were recorded from the LPFC.
source: In this paper, the presence of code-morphing in the LPFC motivated us to analyze the 226 single neurons recorded from the LPFC, which did not include those recorded from the FEF.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset size.

claim: Single neurons in the LPFC showed sustained selectivity to target locations during both delay periods.
source: Single neurons in the LPFC showed sustained selectivity to target locations during both delay periods, with some maintaining the same target tuning in both delays (Figure 1c, left), while some changed target tuning from Delay 1 to Delay 2 (Figure 1c, right).
evidence: This is supported by the example neurons shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Some LPFC neurons maintained the same target tuning in both delays.
source: Single neurons in the LPFC showed sustained selectivity to target locations during both delay periods, with some maintaining the same target tuning in both delays (Figure 1c, left), while some changed target tuning from Delay 1 to Delay 2 (Figure 1c, right).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1c, left panel.

claim: Some LPFC neurons changed target tuning from Delay 1 to Delay 2.
source: Single neurons in the LPFC showed sustained selectivity to target locations during both delay periods, with some maintaining the same target tuning in both delays (Figure 1c, left), while some changed target tuning from Delay 1 to Delay 2 (Figure 1c, right).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1c, right panel.

claim: Neurons with non-linearly mixed selectivity drove code-morphing in the LPFC.
source: The latter category of neurons was characterized as non-linearly mixed selective neurons and was shown to drive code-morphing in the LPFC (Parthasarathy et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Most of the cells with target selectivity in one delay also showed selectivity in the other delay.
source: On the population level, most of the cells with target selectivity in one delay also showed selectivity in the other delay (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 1d.

claim: A decoder trained in Delay 1 could not be used to decode memory locations during Delay 2, and vice versa.
source: We previously reported that the presentation of the distractor led to code-morphing in the LPFC (which was not observed in the FEF), such that a decoder trained in the delay period that preceded the distractor (Delay 1) could not be used to decode memory locations during the delay period that followed the distractor (Delay 2), and vice versa (Parthasarathy et al., 2017; Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by the cross-temporal decoding results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: There were two stable population codes in the LPFC, one in Delay 1 and one in Delay 2, but they did not generalize to each other.
source: In other words, there were two stable population codes in the LPFC, one in Delay 1 and one in Delay 2, but they did not generalize to each other.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the code-morphing results.

claim: Code-morphing was observed in the LPFC but not in the FEF.
source: We previously reported that the presentation of the distractor led to code-morphing in the LPFC (which was not observed in the FEF), such that a decoder trained in the delay period that preceded the distractor (Delay 1) could not be used to decode memory locations during the delay period that followed the distractor (Delay 2), and vice versa (Parthasarathy et al., 2017; Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a claim about regional differences, supported by citation.

claim: Significant information about the target was present outside of the stable working memory subspace.
source: However, significant information about the target was present outside of this space (null space decoding performance of 35.7 ± 1.7% in Delay 1, and 31.6 ± 1.5% in Delay 2) (Parthasarathy, 2019) suggesting the existence of a non-trivial additional subspace that contains target information.
evidence: This is supported by null space decoding performance values cited from previous work.

claim: The existence of a non-trivial additional subspace that contains target information is suggested by information present outside the stable working memory subspace.
source: However, significant information about the target was present outside of this space (null space decoding performance of 35.7 ± 1.7% in Delay 1, and 31.6 ± 1.5% in Delay 2) (Parthasarathy, 2019) suggesting the existence of a non-trivial additional subspace that contains target information.
evidence: This is an inference based on the null space decoding results.

claim: The stable population activity in Delay 2 suggested that the animals could have initiated preparatory activity right after distractor offset.
source: The stable population activity in Delay 2 suggested that the animals could have initiated preparatory activity right after distractor offset, as the distractor was the last signal that reliably predicted the Go cue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics of population activity.

claim: The distractor was the last signal that reliably predicted the Go cue.
source: The stable population activity in Delay 2 suggested that the animals could have initiated preparatory activity right after distractor offset, as the distractor was the last signal that reliably predicted the Go cue.
evidence: This is a statement about the task structure.

claim: The original Delay 1 and Delay 2 activity exhibited 0.33 bits of mutual information.
source: The original Delay 1 and Delay 2 activity exhibited 0.33 bits of mutual information.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the mutual information analysis.

claim: Two unmixed elements were found from D1 and D2 activity with a minimum mutual information of 0.08 bits.
source: Using our method, we found two unmixed elements (representations of unmixed population activity that were each of size 226 × 7) from D1 and D2 activity with a minimum mutual information of 0.08 bits (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the unmixing optimization.

claim: The magnitude of Element 1 in Delay 2 was 65% of that in Delay 1.
source: The two elements we identified consisted of seven vectors in the 226-dimensional space, and according to the unmixing coefficients we identified, the magnitude of one element (Element 1) in Delay 2 was 65% of that in Delay 1, and the magnitude of the other element (Element 2) in Delay 1 was 12% of that in Delay 2.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the unmixing analysis.

claim: The magnitude of Element 2 in Delay 1 was 12% of that in Delay 2.
source: The two elements we identified consisted of seven vectors in the 226-dimensional space, and according to the unmixing coefficients we identified, the magnitude of one element (Element 1) in Delay 2 was 65% of that in Delay 1, and the magnitude of the other element (Element 2) in Delay 1 was 12% of that in Delay 2.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the unmixing analysis.

claim: The magnitude of activity in Subspace 1 increased early after target presentation and was maintained until the saccade cue.
source: The temporal dynamics of the full-space population activity projected into these subspaces showed that the magnitude of activity in Subspace 1 increased early after target presentation and was maintained until the saccade cue, while the magnitude of activity in Subspace 2 increased after distractor presentation and stayed relatively high even after the Go cue (Figure 2c, single-session results are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the projection magnitude plot in Figure 2c.

claim: The magnitude of activity in Subspace 2 increased after distractor presentation and stayed relatively high even after the Go cue.
source: The temporal dynamics of the full-space population activity projected into these subspaces showed that the magnitude of activity in Subspace 1 increased early after target presentation and was maintained until the saccade cue, while the magnitude of activity in Subspace 2 increased after distractor presentation and stayed relatively high even after the Go cue (Figure 2c, single-session results are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the projection magnitude plot in Figure 2c.

claim: Information in Subspace 1 emerged right after target presentation and was present throughout the whole trial, even during the distractor period.
source: Cross-temporal decoding after projecting the full-space neural activity into Subspace 1 showed that information emerged right after target presentation, and although the information was higher in Delay 1 (60.5 ± 1.3%), it was present throughout the whole trial, even during the distractor period (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is shown in the cross-temporal decoding results in Figure 2d.

claim: Information in Subspace 1 was higher in Delay 1 (60.5 ± 1.3%) than in Delay 2 (39.9 ± 1.1%).
source: Cross-temporal decoding after projecting the full-space neural activity into Subspace 1 showed that information emerged right after target presentation, and although the information was higher in Delay 1 (60.5 ± 1.3%), it was present throughout the whole trial, even during the distractor period (Figure 2d). This was qualitatively consistent with our hypothesis, aside from the decrease in information in Delay 2 (39.9 ± 1.1%).
evidence: These are quantitative decoding performance values from Figure 2d.

claim: Information in Subspace 2 emerged after distractor presentation (42.6 ± 1.1%) and was stable throughout Delay 2.
source: Cross-temporal decoding of full-space neural activity projected into Subspace 2 showed that information emerged after distractor presentation (42.6 ± 1.1%), and was stable throughout Delay 2 (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is shown in the cross-temporal decoding results in Figure 2e.

claim: In Delay 1, Subspace 1 and Subspace 2 accounted for 14.6% and 10.3% of the variance in the full space.
source: In Delay 1, Subspace 1 and Subspace 2 accounted for 14.6% and 10.3% of the variance in the full space; in Delay 2, Subspace 1 and Subspace 2 accounted for 5.8% and 8.1% of the variance in the full space.
evidence: These are quantitative variance explained values.

claim: In Delay 2, Subspace 1 and Subspace 2 accounted for 5.8% and 8.1% of the variance in the full space.
source: In Delay 1, Subspace 1 and Subspace 2 accounted for 14.6% and 10.3% of the variance in the full space; in Delay 2, Subspace 1 and Subspace 2 accounted for 5.8% and 8.1% of the variance in the full space.
evidence: These are quantitative variance explained values.

claim: Full-space data in the two subspaces had an effective dimensionality of 6 dimensions each.
source: Full-space data in the two subspaces had an effective dimensionality of 6 dimensions each – after projecting single-trial full-space data into the subspaces, we performed a PCA on the projected data, and the first six out of the seven principal components cumulatively accounted for more than 95% of the variance within each subspace (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The true dimensionality of the neural code could be smaller than the number of discrete target locations imposed by the experiment.
source: This indicated that the true dimensionality of the neural code could be smaller than the number of discrete target locations imposed by the experiment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effective dimensionality being less than 7.

claim: Subspace 1 was significantly closer than chance to the working memory subspace previously described.
source: We found that Subspace 1 was significantly closer than chance to the working memory subspace, while Subspace 2 was not (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on principal angle analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Subspace 2 was not significantly closer than chance to the working memory subspace previously described.
source: We found that Subspace 1 was significantly closer than chance to the working memory subspace, while Subspace 2 was not (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on principal angle analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 45% of LPFC neurons recorded were selective in the period between the Go cue and saccade onset.
source: Activity between the Go cue and the saccade onset contained information about saccade execution (45% of LPFC neurons we recorded were selective in the period between the Go cue and saccade onset, assessed using a one-way ANOVA, p < 0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from ANOVA analysis.

claim: Element 1 and Element 1' were significantly correlated (r > 0.99, p < 0.01).
source: We found that Element 1 and Element 1' were significantly correlated (Figure 3a left, Pearson correlation r > 0.99, p < 0.01).
evidence: This is a quantitative correlation result shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Element 2 and Element 2' were significantly correlated (r = 0.62, p < 0.01).
source: Importantly, Element 2 and Element 2' were also significantly correlated (Figure 3a right, Pearson correlation r = 0.62, p < 0.01).
evidence: This is a quantitative correlation result shown in Figure 3a.

claim: 47% of neurons with spatial tuning in both Delay 2 and the pre-saccade period showed significant correlation between unmixed motor preparation activity and unmixed pre-saccade activity.
source: We found that 47% of these neurons showed significant correlation (Pearson correlation, p < 0.05), which exceeded the number expected by chance (Figure 3b, left bar, p < 0.001, g = 10.82).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-cell correlation analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There was no evidence of a higher number of correlated cells than expected by chance between unmixed working memory activity and unmixed pre-saccade activity.
source: As a control, we carried out the same analysis between the unmixed working memory activity and the unmixed pre-saccade activity, and found no evidence of a higher number of correlated cells than expected by chance (Figure 3b, right bar, p > 0.19, g = 1.51).
evidence: This is a negative result from the control analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between the loading weights in the working memory and motor preparation subspaces (r = 0.68).
source: In addition, to our surprise, we found a significant positive correlation between the loading weights in each subspace (r = 0.68, which was significantly higher than the 95th percentile of 1,000 shuffles, where in each shuffle we randomly permuted the population's loading weights for both subspaces)
evidence: This is a quantitative correlation result from the loading weight analysis.

claim: Neurons with stronger contribution to the working memory subspace would also have a stronger contribution to the motor preparation subspace.
source: which not only supported the second mechanism, but further suggested that neurons with stronger contribution to the working memory subspace would also have a stronger contribution to the motor preparation subspace.
evidence: This is an inference based on the positive correlation between loading weights.

claim: Only 14 (6%) of the neurons had 'exclusive' loading for the working memory or motor preparation subspaces.
source: We found that only 14 (6%) of the neurons had 'exclusive' loading for the working memory (red) or motor preparation (blue) subspaces.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the loading weight distribution analysis.

claim: Neurons with exclusive loading were not necessary to identify the subspaces.
source: However, these cells were not necessary to identify the subspaces (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: All the principal angles between the working memory and motor preparation subspaces were significantly smaller than chance.
source: All the principal angles between the working memory and motor preparation subspaces were significantly smaller than chance, indicating non-orthogonality between the two subspaces and the likelihood of interference of information between them.
evidence: This is based on principal angle analysis comparing to random subspaces.

claim: The working memory and motor preparation subspaces are non-orthogonal.
source: All the principal angles between the working memory and motor preparation subspaces were significantly smaller than chance, indicating non-orthogonality between the two subspaces and the likelihood of interference of information between them.
evidence: This is an inference based on the principal angle analysis.

claim: There is a likelihood of interference of information between the working memory and motor preparation subspaces.
source: All the principal angles between the working memory and motor preparation subspaces were significantly smaller than chance, indicating non-orthogonality between the two subspaces and the likelihood of interference of information between them.
evidence: This is an inference based on the non-orthogonality of the subspaces.

claim: There was no evidence of a drop in decoding performance between projMSub(M) and projMSub(M+P) (p > 0.73, g = 0.61).
source: We found no evidence of a drop in performance between projMSub(M) and projMSub(M+P) (p > 0.73, g = 0.61), and between projPSub(P) and projPSub(M+P) (p > 0.22, g = 2.63), suggesting a lack of interference between these subspaces.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the interference analysis.

claim: There was no evidence of a drop in decoding performance between projPSub(P) and projPSub(M+P) (p > 0.22, g = 2.63).
source: We found no evidence of a drop in performance between projMSub(M) and projMSub(M+P) (p > 0.73, g = 0.61), and between projPSub(P) and projPSub(M+P) (p > 0.22, g = 2.63), suggesting a lack of interference between these subspaces.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the interference analysis.

claim: There was a small decrease (7.1%) of the inter-to-intra cluster distance ratio when both working memory and motor preparation activity were projected into the subspaces.
source: We found a small decrease (7.1%) of the inter-to-intra cluster distance ratio when both working memory and motor preparation activity were projected into the subspaces, suggesting the existence of a small, but significant interference between both subspaces (p < 0.001, g = 4.81 between projMSub(M) and projMSub(M+P), p < 0.001, g = 6.63 between projPSub(P) and projPSub(M+P)).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the state space interference analysis.

claim: There is a small, but significant interference between the working memory and motor preparation subspaces.
source: We found a small decrease (7.1%) of the inter-to-intra cluster distance ratio when both working memory and motor preparation activity were projected into the subspaces, suggesting the existence of a small, but significant interference between both subspaces (p < 0.001, g = 4.81 between projMSub(M) and projMSub(M+P), p < 0.001, g = 6.63 between projPSub(P) and projPSub(M+P)).
evidence: This is an inference based on the inter-to-intra cluster distance ratio analysis.

claim: Decoding performance was significantly reduced in error trials in the working memory subspace compared to correct trials (p < 0.001, g = 13.9).
source: Decoding performance was significantly reduced in error trials (Figure 5a,) compared to correct trials (Figure 5a, p < 0.001, g = 13.9 between projMSub(M) and projMSub(ME)), suggesting that failures in memory encoding occurred during error trials.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the error trial analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Failures in memory encoding occurred during error trials.
source: Decoding performance was significantly reduced in error trials (Figure 5a,) compared to correct trials (Figure 5a, p < 0.001, g = 13.9 between projMSub(M) and projMSub(ME)), suggesting that failures in memory encoding occurred during error trials.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced decoding performance in error trials.

claim: Decoding performance was significantly reduced in error trials in the motor preparation subspace compared to correct trials (p < 0.001, g = 13.8).
source: A similar analysis on the motor preparation subspace yielded equivalent results (Figure 5b, p < 0.001, g = 13.8 between projPSub(P) and projPSub(PE)), which were consistent with the fact that in error trials, saccades were made to different locations than in correct trials.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the error trial analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In error trials, saccades were made to different locations than in correct trials.
source: A similar analysis on the motor preparation subspace yielded equivalent results (Figure 5b, p < 0.001, g = 13.8 between projPSub(P) and projPSub(PE)), which were consistent with the fact that in error trials, saccades were made to different locations than in correct trials.
evidence: This is a statement about behavioral performance in error trials.

claim: The subspaces found could have been used by the animals to perform the task.
source: These results suggested that the subspaces we found could have been used by the animals to perform the task.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral relevance shown in error trials.

claim: The mean population firing rate did not change between Delay 1, Delay 2 and pre-target fixation periods.
source: In addition, we noticed that the mean population firing rate did not change between Delay 1, Delay 2 and pre-target fixation periods (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The observation of constant mean population firing rate was consistent with a population normalization mechanism to maintain the mean population firing rate at a constant level in the LPFC.
source: This observation was consistent with a population normalization mechanism to maintain the mean population firing rate at a constant level in the LPFC (Ruff and Cohen, 2017; Duong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous work on normalization.

claim: Only the attractor model with divisive normalization qualitatively replicated all the features of the neural data.
source: We found that only the attractor model with divisive normalization qualitatively replicated all the features of the neural data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only the linear subspace model with divisive normalization replicated all the main findings in the neural data.
source: Similarly, only the linear subspace model with divisive normalization replicated all the main findings in the neural data (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Divisive normalization was needed to faithfully replicate the properties of neural data.
source: The results of the model simulations supported the idea that divisive normalization was needed to faithfully replicate the properties of neural data, and suggested that such a mechanism constituted part of the function of the LPFC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: Divisive normalization constitutes part of the function of the LPFC.
source: The results of the model simulations supported the idea that divisive normalization was needed to faithfully replicate the properties of neural data, and suggested that such a mechanism constituted part of the function of the LPFC.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the modeling results.

claim: Working memory and motor preparation subspaces coexist in a single neural network within the LPFC.
source: Overall, our results show that working memory and motor preparation subspaces coexist in a single neural network within the LPFC.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: This work provides the first evidence suggesting that information about two separate cognitive processes can be simultaneously encoded in subspaces within the same brain region.
source: Our results provided the first evidence suggesting that information about two separate cognitive processes can be simultaneously encoded in subspaces within the same brain region.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The majority of the literature on information subspaces in the brain has reported a single subspace.
source: The majority of the literature on information subspaces in the brain has reported a single subspace (Parthasarathy, 2019; Druckmann and Chklovskii, 2012; Inagaki et al., 2019; Svoboda and Li, 2018), multiple subspaces in different regions (Semedo et al., 2019), or multiple subspaces in the same region where information transited from one subspace to another but did not coexist simultaneously in different subspaces (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016; Yoo and Hayden, 2020; Kimmel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mante et al., 2013 showed coexistence of information in three subspaces in the prefrontal cortex, but two of the subspaces encoded color and motion (stimulus subspace), and only one subspace encoded action choice (cognitive subspace).
source: Mante et al., 2013. showed coexistence of information in three subspaces in the prefrontal cortex, but two of the subspaces encoded color and motion (stimulus subspace), and only one subspace encoded action choice (cognitive subspace).
evidence: This is a description of previous work, supported by citation.

claim: Minxha et al., 2020 reported the existence of two cognitive subspaces for 'memory' and 'categorization' tasks, but the two subspaces were employed asynchronously in different types of trial blocks.
source: Minxha et al., 2020. reported the existence of two cognitive subspaces for 'memory' and 'categorization' tasks, but the two subspaces were employed asynchronously in different types of trial blocks.
evidence: This is a description of previous work, supported by citation.
